item.title: @fordjourstudio: Inspired by the dubious mystery surrounding the tragic death of Nolan Wells, Fishing Trip
item.author: @fordjourstudio
item.description:
Inspired by the dubious mystery surrounding the tragic death of Nolan Wells, Fishing Trip is at once an ideal image of racial progress in a state fraught with a brutal history of racial animus and at the same time, a black parent’s worst nightmare.
Invoking both art historical and biblical themes of martyrdom: from the betrayal of Christ, Joseph and his coat of many colors to momento mori with the offering of dead fish, a leisurely boat ride becomes the staging of a dramatic scene foreshadowing a murder mystery of epic proportions.

item.title: [Opening] @caseykaplangallery: Now open, HANNAH LEVY’S third solo exhibition at the gallery “Boiled,” on view through Jan
item.author: @caseykaplangallery
item.description:
Now open, HANNAH LEVY’S third solo exhibition at the gallery “Boiled,” on view through January 9th.
Seven new sculptures examine the uneasy relationship between the body and the designed world through visceral material interactions.
Combining blown glass with hand-carved and polished stainless steel, Levy draws on the anatomies of arthropods and serpents alongside references to: furniture, Art Nouveau ornamentation, and mobility aids.
Bubbling glass in warm, organic hues is blown through, encased, and compressed by jointed limbs, pointed extremities, and sinuous supports.
Her creature-object hybrids hover between defense and vulnerability, playing with the inherent tensions of the structures and systems designed to support, protect, transport, and treat the body.
Both elegant and unsettling, Levy’s sculptures serve as sensuous reminders of precarious negotiations–ornament and function, care and constraint, flesh and mechanism–making tangible how designed forms accommodate and constrain the bodies they encounter.

item.title: [Opening] @caseykaplangallery: Now open, ELLA WALKER’S third solo exhibition at the gallery “The Street,” on view through
item.author: @caseykaplangallery
item.description:
Now open, ELLA WALKER’S third solo exhibition at the gallery “The Street,” on view through January 9th.
“The Street,” a new body of work roused from a lucid dream of remembered places and human intrigue set halfway between the Renaissance and present day.
Across five large scale paintings, a cast of characters move through brick-lined streets with uncanny spatial logic, fragmenting their bodies into a palimpsest of limbs, faces, and disembodied hands.
Layered and diluted paint flows in translucent swathes of color dammed by assertive outlines, occasionally revealing the ghostly pentimenti of an altered pose or worked-over figure.
Introducing contemporary costumes and observed environments, Walker’s expanded visual language grounds and reinvents the drama of an interior self set loose in the outside world.
Installation view:
“Roman Street” 2026 Acrylic dispersion, pigment, chalk and pencil on linen 71 x 106.5” / 180.3 x 270.5cm
Reading like a frieze around the perimeter of the gallery, the horizontal and vertical tableaus rally across pictorial space, shuttling the viewer between public settings and private rooms.

item.author: @alminerech
item.description:
Happy birthday to Ji Xin(@jixiiin)! To celebrate, we start with spotlighting his artwork ‘Tower 塔’(2026), recently featured at our booth at Art Basel Paris 2026. We then look back at his most recent show with the gallery, ’Moonlight · Butterfly’ at Almine Rech Paris in 2023. We end with three institutional shows, ‘The Gaze of Pygmalion’ at the Long Museum (West Bund) in Shanghai, China in 2025, ‘A Cloud in Trousers: Painting Today’ at the West Bund Museum in Shanghai, China in 2024 and ‘Boundless Reverie: Chinese Savoir-Faire and Contemporary Art’ at K11 Art & Cultural Centre in Hong Kong in 2024!
•
Ji Xin portrays the homogeneous representations of complex emotions shared by the collective that can travel through time, examining the hustle and bustle in the void, demonstrating a grasp of the seemingly innocent but subtle atmosphere of his works.
Ji Xin‘s creations were born out of the search for classical, innocent, delicate, and mysterious complexities. In this process, the artist draws on external nutrients, cutting out the self in his work and presenting the figure as a detached reality. In perceiving changes in the outside world, the artist has pursued familiar techniques while creating idealized worlds, playing with surrealism and detachment, all while keeping a clear link to reality. Ji Xin attempts to distill a metaphysical reference through the setting of figures and scenarios, revealing a reverted state of coexistence between man and god.

item.description:
Resilience of Messages to the Storm
Artistic Director Norwood “PJ” Pennewell of Garth Fagan Dance explains the meaning behind the closing piece of the show, Messages To The Storm by Executive Director Natalie Rogers-Cropper. The dance follows hope and optimism as they grow into full-blown resilience, and Rogers-Cropper sums it up with a line from Maya Angelou: “Every storm runs out of rain.” Pennewell adds that the piece is designed to reach younger audiences with a message that, despite technology and especially AI, the human element is where art truly comes from.
Garth Fagan Dance, based in Rochester, is at The Joyce Theater November 4-8, 2026, for its 55th season, with its signature fusion of modern, post-modern, Afro-Caribbean, and ballet influences. The company honors Distinguished Artistic Director Emeritus Garth Fagan, recipient of the 2025 Bessie Award for Lifetime Achievement and the Tony Award-winning choreographer behind Disney’s The Lion King, with an electrifying evening of rhythm, rigor, and soul. Program highlights include Fagan’s seminal Prelude: Discipline is Freedom and the evocative Never Top 40, returning to New York City for the first time since 2001. Two NYC premieres expand the company’s bold artistic vision: Priestess Hill by Pennewell and Messages To The Storm by Rogers-Cropper.

item.author: @christiesinc
item.description:
Andy Warhol spent his career turning others into icons. In his final years, he turned that same vision upon himself.
Painted in 1986, just months before his death, Warhol's monumental ‘Self-Portrait’ presents the artist on a larger-than-life scale. With his unmistakable 'fright wig' and penetrating gaze, Warhol confronts the viewer directly, yet reveals remarkably little of the man behind his carefully constructed public persona.
Michael Baptist, Vice President and Specialist of Post-War and Contemporary Art, explores how this striking work reflects Warhol's lifelong fascination with image-making and his ability to secure his own place in American cultural history.

item.title: @marianneboeskygallery: For A Woman of Will, Michaela Yearwood-Dan transforms the gallery into a sanctuary for rei
item.author: @marianneboeskygallery
item.description:
For A Woman of Will, Michaela Yearwood-Dan transforms the gallery into a sanctuary for reimagining the collective practices of love, care, and liberation. A Woman of Will coincides with Yearwood-Dan’s first UK solo institutional exhibition, The Practice of Liberation, which debuted at The Whitworth in Manchester in April and will travel to the Towner in Eastbourne and the Arnolfini in Bristol.
For A Woman of Will, Yearwood-Dan conjures the cool, sacred atmosphere of a cathedral. A suite of 13 small paintings—one for each of Jesus’ apostles, including Mary Magdalene—line the walls of the gallery’s small front room, evoking the intimacy of a side chapel. Throughout the airy gallery, large-scale paintings—lush, gestural abstractions in vivid cobalts, gold, and maroons—evoke sunlight streaming through stained-glass windows. Diaristic meditations and small objects—ceramic petals, glass beads, glitter, gold leaf, paper scraps, and neatly-tied ribbons—adorn the paintings’ surfaces. Small bronze-lustered, hand-built ceramic vases—filled with dried flowers—dot the deep burgundy walls between paintings, the faint floral scent reminiscent of incense. Throughout the space, ornate, ceramic-tiled wood benches—made in collaboration with sculptor and furniture designer Theodore Vass—serve as pews, offering respite for quiet contemplation.
A Woman of Will will be on on view through December 12 at Boesky Gallery in New York.
📸 Jason Wyche

One thing that stands out about the 1984 revival of Einstein on the Beach is that director Robert Wilson himself took the stage in the "Flashlight Dance." Revived 8 years after it debuted at the Festival d'Avignon, the piece was originally choreographed by Byrd Hoffman dancer Andy DeGroat. Lucinda Childs re-envisioned the movement in its 1984 revival, commissioned by BAM, and her choreography was likewise used in the 1992 and 2012 revivals. Wilson directed all four of these productions, starting with the original in 1976, so performing Childs' version in the production's American debut is quite a compliment.
In celebration of the milestone, this November we're proud to present Einstein on the Beach–50th Anniversary Concert with by the artists who know it best—The Philip Glass Ensemble, led by longtime music director Michael Riesman—with a special artistic installation by Tony and Olivier Award-winning artist and designer Es Devlin inspired by Glass’s early writings about his mesmerizing music.

item.author: @lorraineogradytrust
item.description:
Now open: MoMA PS1 presents “Hard Art,” a major exhibition examining the legacy of abstract painting by Black artists in the United States from 1969 to the present, featuring Lorraine O’Grady’s “Landscape (Western Hemisphere)” (2010–11).
Bringing together more than forty artists across three generations, “Hard Art” traces the evolution of abstraction through historical paintings and contemporary practices spanning sculpture, video, sound, and painting. Featured artists include Frank Bowling, Mark Bradford, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Ed Clark, Melvin Edwards, Jennie C. Jones, and Lorraine O’Grady, alongside Aria Dean, Torkwase Dyson, Nikita Gale, Suzanne Jackson, and others.
O’Grady’s “Landscape (Western Hemisphere)” (2010–11) is an 18-minute, single-channel video in which close-up images of the artist’s hair, animated by fans, transform into a shifting abstract landscape. Accompanied by the sounds of birds, insects, wind, and urban environments, the work considers hair as a metaphor for the hybridity of the Western Hemisphere, reflecting on race, cultural mixing, colonial histories, and the Black female body.
In the exhibition catalogue, Connie Butler, Director of MoMA PS1 and curator of “Hard Art,” dedicates the project to O’Grady, acknowledging the enduring influence of her practice: “This project is dedicated to Lorraine O’Grady, whose legacy of radicality, brilliance, and capacity for disruption lives on and inspires so many of us.”

item.title: [Opening] @ellerustle: Went to see Pollock/Krasner at the Met with EA.
item.author: @ellerustle
item.description:
Went to see Pollock/Krasner at the Met with EA. Everyone seemed surprised to see a three year old in the galleries and EA was cheered to have an audience tune in and chuckle at his commentary.
Clement Greenberg comes up again and again, but never with real depth. There’s little for a general audience on what Greenberg stood for (or didn’t), or on what it meant for Abstract Expressionism to be upheld through Pollock’s imagination. Krasner was rigorous and seeing so much of her work in physical space was moving; as with many heteronormative relationships it’s as if there is this undercurrent of assumption that these women were necessarily martyrs to the “masters” of art history, and therefore their being eclipsed was some kind of service to the cultural and intellectual output that their partnership (and putting up with complete and total nonsense that they shouldn’t have had to deal with) sustained, as if their being eclipsed and oppressed was some sort of community service to all of us hereafter in the currents of history now.
The timing is complicated. *Hard Art* opens this week at MoMA PS1, a group show tracing the lineage of Black artists within abstract painting. Pollock lived alongside many of the artists in that history and never formally acknowledged their influence. It’s hard to believe he wasn’t aware of them; especially because he was indisputably an unpleasant jerk who likely would have hated sharing space with other planets in this art historical constellation.
The Met points to Picasso and Modigliani, but both were themselves deeply influenced by African art, a lineage the show doesn’t pursue. Nor does it grapple with the political moment this work came out of, or what that moment did to peerships within a segregated art history.
I hope everyone who seeks out Pollock/Krasner also goes to *Hard Art*. These histories have so often been taught separately, and Greenberg in particular never bridged them in a way that lent toward any real structural rigor. However it’s important to remember as these two major museums send signals in telling these stories that these histories in fact always converge, and they need to be narrated in the round.

Opening day of HANNAH LEVY’S “Boiled,” happening this evening Thursday November 5th, from: 6-8pm.
Seven new sculptures examine the uneasy relationship between the body and the designed world through visceral material interactions.
Combining blown glass with hand-carved and polished stainless steel, Levy draws on the anatomies of arthropods and serpents alongside references to: furniture, Art Nouveau ornamentation, and mobility aids.
Bubbling glass in warm, organic hues is blown through, encased, and compressed by jointed limbs, pointed extremities, and sinuous supports.
Her creature-object hybrids hover between defense and vulnerability, playing with the inherent tensions of the structures and systems designed to support, protect, transport, and treat the body.
Both elegant and unsettling, Levy’s sculptures serve as sensuous reminders of precarious negotiations–ornament and function, care and constraint, flesh and mechanism–making tangible how designed forms accommodate and constrain the bodies they encounter.

“The Street,” a new body of work roused from a lucid dream of remembered places and human intrigue set halfway between the Renaissance and present day.
Across five large scale paintings, a cast of characters move through brick-lined streets with uncanny spatial logic, fragmenting their bodies into a palimpsest of limbs, faces, and disembodied hands.
Layered and diluted paint flows in translucent swathes of color dammed by assertive outlines, occasionally revealing the ghostly pentimenti of an altered pose or worked-over figure.
Introducing contemporary costumes and observed environments, Walker’s expanded visual language grounds and reinvents the drama of an interior self set loose in the outside world.
Image:
“Action” 2026 Acrylic dispersion, pigment, chalk and pencil on linen 70.75 x 63.5” / 179.7 x 161.3cm
Reading like a frieze around the perimeter of the gallery, the horizontal and vertical tableaus rally across pictorial space, shuttling the viewer between public settings and private rooms.

Almine Rech Shanghai is pleased to announce ‘The Greatness of the Everyday’, Tom Wesselmann’s first solo exhibition in mainland China, on view from November 9, 2026 to January 9, 2027.
@tom_wesselmann

Spanning over four decades, this exhibition illuminates the progression of Wesselmann’s oeuvre and the bodies of work that defined it, from the origins of his Great American Nude series to his late-career Sunset Nudes. While Wesselmann was driven by constant aesthetic and material innovation, he also had a tendency to return ceaselessly to certain themes and motifs, engaging with art history, his predecessors, and even as his own earlier output. As the artist explained: “When I made the decision in 1959 that I was not going to be an abstract painter, that I was going to be a representational painter, I had absolutely no enthusiasm about any particular subject or direction or anything. I was starting from absolute zero. And in choosing representational painting, I decided to do, as my subject matter, the history of art: I would do nudes, still lives, landscapes, interiors, portraits, etc. It didn’t take long before I began to follow my most active interests: nudes and still lifes.”
— Tom Wesselmann, in Marco Livingstone, “Telling it like it is,” Tom Wesselmann: A Retrospective Survey 1959 to 1993, Cantz Editions, 1996, p. 10.

item.description:
Taylor Thursday: “Esplanade” ✨
Sometimes the most ordinary movements can become something extraordinary.
Created in 1975, “Esplanade” grew out of Paul Taylor’s fascination with everyday movement. Inspired by the sight of a woman running for a bus, Taylor built the work from walking, running, falling, and simple gestures, transforming familiar actions into sweeping patterns of movement set to music by Johann Sebastian Bach.
Playful, romantic, somber, and explosive all at once, “Esplanade” became one of Taylor’s most celebrated works and remains a defining example of his ability to find beauty, emotion, and possibility in the everyday.
Taylor’s choreography also mirrors the structure of Bach’s music, layering and repeating movement phrases much like the overlapping melodic lines found throughout the score.
Last performed by the Company in New York City in 2025 at the David H. Koch Theater, “Esplanade” returns this November as part of the 2026 New York Season.
📅 November 6, 10, 18, 21 (EVE) 🎟️ Tickets are available at the link in bio.
Have you seen “Esplanade” onstage before? We’d love to hear your favorite memories of this beloved Taylor work. 💫
As we wrap up our Taylor Thursday series, thank you for joining us as we revisited some of Paul Taylor’s most memorable works from across the years. We hope you’ve enjoyed looking back with us, and that you’ll have the chance to experience some of these dances live during the 2026 New York Season. We can’t wait to welcome you to the theater! 👏

item.description:
Mary Lovelace O'Neal: Requiem—the artist's first posthumous exhibition—features a selection of work by Mary Lovelace O’Neal from the 1980s and 1990s, the period in which the artist honed her rich, personal iconography.
Requiem chronicles a transformative time in Lovelace O’Neal’s career, both personally and artistically. Settling in the Bay Area at the tail end of the 1970s, Lovelace O’Neal established an illustrious academic career and embarked on an extensive agenda of international travel throughout the 1980s and 1990s. In California, the hint of submerged color that had appeared throughout the artist’s early, minimalist-inspired lampblack paintings burst forth from their erstwhile restraints. An expressionistic impulse—first discovered in David Driskell’s class at Howard University—reemerged in grand, physical gestures. As she wove childhood memories and visions of distant lands into her ongoing investigation of color and abstraction, the artist’s distinct visual language began to coalesce. A cast of imagined characters—“whales and mermaids, little pigs and butterflies, panthers and white doves”—percolating in the recesses of Lovelace O’Neal’s mind came to life on canvas, and a latent sense of narrative emerged across her oeuvre, as if each work embodied a scene from a grand mythology cultivated within the artist’s imagination.
Requiem is on view at Boesky Gallery in New York through December 19.

Gustav Klimt. The Bloch-Bauers. Egon Schiele. These names were part of a flourishing art world in Vienna. Then, with the Anschluss, or the Nazi annexation of Austria of 1938, lives were upended, families were persecuted and works of art disappeared from the collections of those who had commissioned, collected and cherished them.
Lost Vienna: Restitution of a Golden Age explores the stories of Jewish collectors, dealers and the journeys of the works they left behind. Told through the work and lives of Klimt and Schiele, these stories illuminate a lost world — and the legacies that endure.

A Philadelphia artist who refused to be defined by the expectations of her time.
Cecilia Beaux became one of the most celebrated portraitists of her generation, painting writers, artists, political figures, and members of Philadelphia society with an approach that was distinctly her own.
Born and trained in Philadelphia, Beaux studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts before continuing her training in Paris. She later returned to PAFA as its first full-time woman faculty member.
Get to know Cecilia Beaux and her remarkable career in “A Nation of Artists,” on view at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and PAFA.
Across the two museums, "A Nation of Artists" features more than 1,000 works, including more than 120 iconic paintings and decorative arts from the Middleton Family Collection. Together, these works offer fresh perspectives on the evolving story of American art and experience.

Two paintings, two visions of Impressionist Paris.
Here, Sotheby’s Simon Shaw and Samuel Valette return to the city that inspired Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro over a century ago. In ‘Le Jardin des Tuileries,’ Monet presents a luminous panorama of one of Paris’ most famed landmarks. It reveals Monet’s sensitivity to the effects of light and atmosphere, capturing lush greenery in harmony with the surrounding city.
In contrast, Pissarro paints a view of the modern metropolis, capturing the bustling energy of a Parisian boulevard. With its masterful play of light and shadow and rhythmic vitality, the painting stands as a supreme achievement of Impressionism.

ANNOUNCEMENT | Mariane Ibrahim to present Derrick Adams
We are pleased to present the work of Derrick Adams (b. 1970, Baltimore, Maryland; lives and works in Brooklyn, New York), a multidisciplinary artist whose practice celebrates and expands the dialogue around contemporary Black life and culture. This new collaboration will begin with Adams’s first solo exhibition at Mariane Ibrahim in Mexico City, opening during the city’s Art Week in February 2027. The exhibition also marks the beginning of a dialogue between the artist and Mexico, a country whose cultural and artistic histories have long intrigued him.
At the heart of Adams’s practice is the conviction that pleasure can be subversive. Through vibrant colors and playful compositions, his works invite viewers into narratives that gradually reveal their complexity. Visual pleasure becomes a point of entry, a means of engaging audiences in deeper questions about representation, cultural memory, and the histories that shape our understanding of art.

Countdown to the opening of HANNAH LEVY’S “Boiled,” happening tomorrow Thursday November 5th, from: 6-8pm.
Image: (detail)
“Untitled” 2026 Stainless steel, glass 69” (H) x 28” (W) x 15” (D) 175.3 cm (H) x 71.1cm (W) x 38.1cm (D)
Seven new sculptures examine the uneasy relationship between the body and the designed world through visceral material interactions.
Combining blown glass with hand-carved and polished stainless steel, Levy draws on the anatomies of arthropods and serpents alongside references to: furniture, Art Nouveau ornamentation, and mobility aids.
Bubbling glass in warm, organic hues is blown through, encased, and compressed by jointed limbs, pointed extremities, and sinuous supports.
Her creature-object hybrids hover between defense and vulnerability, playing with the inherent tensions of the structures and systems designed to support, protect, transport, and treat the body.
Both elegant and unsettling, Levy’s sculptures serve as sensuous reminders of precarious negotiations–ornament and function, care and constraint, flesh and mechanism–making tangible how designed forms accommodate and constrain the bodies they encounter.
“Hannah Levy: Boiled” is on view at the gallery through January 9, 2027.

item.author: @alminerech

Almine Rech New York is pleased to announce ‘James Turrell: Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue’, James Turrell’s 13th solo exhibition in over three decades with the gallery, on view from November 12, 2026 to January 30, 2027.
@jamesturell
•
On the occasion of the exhibition, we look back on a conversation between Almine Rech and James Turrell, recorded on the train between Brussels and Paris and included in the book ‘Rencontres 9: James Turrell / Almine Rech’:
Almine Rech: You were born in a Quaker family, what are the main characteristics of this religion?
James Turrell: Two aspects, first encounter silence in the service, second going inside to greet the light. This idea of group meditation…
AR: ...is very important?
JT: Yes it is very important. You can talk more or less depending on more sectarian or more liberal meetings.
AR: As a child what difference does it make being in a Quaker family?
JT: It is a strong inculcation. It depends on the meeting again, on the kind of meeting: Conservative or Orthodox.
AR: And you were in....?
JT: A more conservative form. They actually have quite long meetings; that was hard for children, to stay still from one to three hours inside the meeting house. A good meeting would go on three hours or more.
[...]
AR: Do you think the way your parents thought and practiced this religion has influenced your way of thinking, your art?
JT: There was a time when I was very much involved in it, then I came to think it was ridiculous. Now I can realize that I am more influenced by it than I thought.
— Rencontres 9: James Turrell / Almine Rech, Almine Rech Éditions and Éditions Images Modernes, 2005, pp. 10-20.

“The Street,” a new body of work roused from a lucid dream of remembered places and human intrigue set halfway between the Renaissance and present day.
Across five large scale paintings, a cast of characters move through brick-lined streets with uncanny spatial logic, fragmenting their bodies into a palimpsest of limbs, faces, and disembodied hands.
Layered and diluted paint flows in translucent swathes of color dammed by assertive outlines, occasionally revealing the ghostly pentimenti of an altered pose or worked-over figure.
Introducing contemporary costumes and observed environments, Walker’s expanded visual language grounds and reinvents the drama of an interior self set loose in the outside world.

Reading like a frieze around the perimeter of the gallery, the horizontal and vertical tableaus rally across pictorial space, shuttling the viewer between public settings and private rooms.

We hope this Mughal period painting inspires you to decrease your screen time.
Here, Sotheby’s Rukmani Rathore tells the story of this meditative painting from the 17th century. It’s attributed to the imperial Mughal master, Govardhan, whose paintings were defined by their peaceful, spiritual themes. Throughout his life, he painted impressive royal portraits but is better known for his depictions of ascetics, faqirs and mystics such as the one shown here.
‘An elderly mystic and a musician’ is a highlight of the Arts of the Islamic World & India Auction, coming to #SothebysLondon on 10 November. Register to bid at the link in bio.

Ibrahim Said Egyptian-American sculptor Said came from a family who ran a ceramics workshop in Cairo. Said creates intricately hand-carved clay vessels to reference multiple religious and craft traditions of the Middle East: ancient Egyptian, Coptic, and Islamic art come together in works that combine centuries-old, and even millennia-old, patterns and symbols with contemporary forms. Currently showing at @yossimilo and one of three inaugural artists in the Metropolitan Museum of Art- an 18-month residency granted Said sustained access to the Met’s collection, resulting in the development of this body of work.

//INTERVIEW
Osaze Akil Stigler
Osaze Akil Stigler is a Chicago-born, Atlanta-based multidisciplinary artist. His paintings place Black figures in positions of comfort, beauty, and power, and fashion plays a big part in his visual language. His work also reaches into experiential design and spatial storytelling. He is featured in our Best of the Art World editorial.
Q: Fashion plays an important role in your visual language. What does clothing allow you to express about identity and personal choice?
A: Autonomy. It all goes back to the ability to choose how you show up in the world, and how you want the world to encounter you. I think back to the Tignon laws of Louisiana where black women were forced to wear head coverings to cover their natural hair, and in defiance of the law, they made beautifully extravagant headdresses. There’s so much power in that to me.

item.title: @sothebys: This is perhaps the closest thing we have to a Monet family portrait. In 1887, Claude Mone
item.author: @sothebys
item.description:
This is perhaps the closest thing we have to a Monet family portrait. In 1887, Claude Monet began an ambitious series of paintings depicting the young women of his extended family. This suite marked a rare return to figuration at a moment when landscape had become his main subject.
In 1883, Monet settled at Giverny with his second wife Alice Hoschedé and their combined eight children. ‘La Barque bleue’ depicts two of Hoschedé's daughters, believed to be Marthe and Blanche, afloat on the river Epte. Here, Monet uses color, light and reflection to dissolve the boundaries between figure and landscape.
The painting is an achievement in Monet's engagement with the human figure, while foreshadowing the immersive world of his celebrated ‘Nymphéas.’
‘La Barque bleue’ is a highlight of The Modern Evening Auction, presented in partnership with @celine, coming to #SothebysNewYork on 18 November. Register to bid at the link in bio.

item.title: @rebuild_foundation: “A postcard is an open letter, flying across the world, and naked for all to see. It is ca
item.author: @rebuild_foundation
item.description:
“A postcard is an open letter, flying across the world, and naked for all to see. It is cardstock– heavy and light. In a time when truth is as elusive as care, the postcard became an appropriate canvas to investigate who and where we have been. I did not want to disturb history, but bring it to the fore. These are the first songs that revealed themselves to me.” - Yaw Agyeman
As we extend the spirit of American Archives Month, we’re honored to spotlight the work of artists, scholars, and cultural practitioners who have researched in and created new work from the archives and collections under Rebuild’s care.
Mellon Archives Innovation Fellow and Chicago-based interdisciplinary performing artist Yaw Agyeman chose to enter into a delicate dialogue with a collection of postcards contained within the Ed J. Williams Collection of ‘Negrobilia,’ a collection of over 4,000 objects representing harmful and derogatory stereotypes of Black people, amassed with the intention of removing the imagery and ephemera from public circulation. This extended archival conversation inspired his first-ever album, AGORO, a 45 RPM vinyl record published on his 45th birthday. Thank you, Yaw, for this offering, which gives new life to this archive through your work.
Launched in 2022, with the generous support of the @mellonfdn, the Mellon Archives Innovation Fellowship at Rebuild established a multifaceted initiative supporting the creation of new research, scholarship, and artistic production through engagement with Rebuild’s archival collections held at the Stony Island Arts Bank.

Tonight's program is in Indiewire: What are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night? Join Us! Tuesday, November 3rd, 2026 at 7PM Film Screening and Election Night Afterparty ~ FREE!
Co-presented with The NEW MUSEUM ELECTION NIGHT at MAYSLES + BLKNEWS: TERMS AND CONDITIONS
Kahlil Joseph, 2025, 113 min., USA
As America watches the election returns, Maysles Documentary Center invites audiences to experience a different kind of news.
Kahlil Joseph’s BLKNWS: TERMS & CONDITIONS (2025) is a visionary exploration of Black history, memory, and imagination. Combining archival footage, music, contemporary media, and speculative storytelling, Joseph constructs a radical alternative to conventional news and historical narratives, one in which Black life becomes the center rather than the margins of the story.
Co-presented with The New Museum, who presented Khalil Joseph’s exhibition Shadow Play in 2017 and are currently presenting BLKNWS collaborator Arthur Jafa’s major survey exhibition, I Am Tony, the screening highlights artists challenging conventional ways of seeing and representing Black experience, drawing upon the emotional power of images, the rhythms of Black music, and the possibilities of cinema to imagine new forms of collective memory and consciousness.
On a night dominated by electoral maps, political punditry, and competing visions of America’s future, BLKNWS invites us to consider another question: Who gets to tell our stories, and what becomes possible when we control the images?
Join us following the screening for a post-election gathering and celebration at Maysles Documentary Center!

Danielle Mckinney: Shelter opens November 6 at the New Orleans Museum of Art.
Shelter is Mckinney’s largest museum exhibition to date. It offers a collective understanding of the artist’s gift for weaving together art history, emotionally resonant subjects, and beautifully rendered paintings. Layering technique and reference, Mckinney’s sensual interiors become necessary sites of spiritual restoration, proving internal shelter is fostered through authority over one’s own time. Rachel Gustafson; Dr. Imani Perry, Carol K. Pforzheimer Professor at the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University; acclaimed curator and critic Ekow Eshun; and Florida-based visual artist and poet Autumn Kioti Horne.

item.author: @phillipsauction
item.description:
Executed in 1959, ‘Snow Flurry, May 14’ captures Alexander Calder’s masterful dance of harmony and tension innate to the natural world.​
Coming to auction for the first time, the work was a gift from the artist to Mário Pedrosa, the Brazilian critic and an early champion of Calder's, who helped organize his first solo exhibition in Rio de Janeiro in 1948. The show had a galvanizing impact, drawing Calder into dialogue with Lygia Clark, Oscar Niemeyer, and a generation of Brazilian artists shaping their own modern idiom.​
A singular artifact of a transnational friendship, the mobile belongs to a vital chapter in the history of modernism, when dialogues across continents expanded the horizons of postwar art.​

item.description: This year, @parisphotofair marks the Bicentennial of Photography at the Grand Palais, and we’re honored to take part with a solo presentation of silver gelatin prints by Joseph Szabo.⁠ ⁠ The booth brings together renowned and unseen photographs from the 1960s–1990s, including vintage prints from the artist’s archive and several large-scale works. Our presentation coincides with the launch of “American Teen” (@importantflowers / @mack_publishing), a new monograph edited by @sofiacoppola.⁠ ⁠ For more than twenty-five years, Szabo taught high school art and photography, using his camera to connect with his students and gaining access to a teenage world most adults never see. His images of rebellion, self-expression, and first love have influenced a generation of photographers, musicians, and filmmakers, from Bruce Weber and Juergen Teller to Cameron Crowe and Coppola herself. “Priscilla” (1969) became the cover of Dinosaur Jr.’s “Green Mind,” and “The Kiss” (1977) was named by @nytimes one of the 25 most influential fashion photographs of the past century.⁠ ⁠ This is Jackson Fine Art's first solo presentation of Szabo’s work at Paris Photo.⁠ ⁠ 📍 Grand Palais, Paris | Booth C10⁠ ⁠ Head to the link in our bio to view the full collection ↖️

Installation is ongoing for HANNAH LEVY’S upcoming third solo exhibition “Boiled,” opening next Thursday November 5th, from: 6-8pm, and on view at the gallery through January 9th.
Image: (detail)
“Untitled” 2026 Stainless steel, glass 78” (H) x 30” (W) x 11.5” (D) 198.12cm (H) x 76.2cm (W) x 29.21cm (D)
Seven new sculptures examine the uneasy relationship between the body and the designed world through visceral material interactions.
Combining blown glass with hand-carved and polished stainless steel, Levy draws on the anatomies of arthropods and serpents alongside references to: furniture, Art Nouveau ornamentation, and mobility aids.
Bubbling glass in warm, organic hues is blown through, encased, and compressed by jointed limbs, pointed extremities, and sinuous supports.
Her creature-object hybrids hover between defense and vulnerability, playing with the inherent tensions of the structures and systems designed to support, protect, transport, and treat the body.
Both elegant and unsettling, Levy’s sculptures serve as sensuous reminders of precarious negotiations–ornament and function, care and constraint, flesh and mechanism–making tangible how designed forms accommodate and constrain the bodies they encounter.

Nate Lewis (@nloois) is a New York-based artist whose practice grew out of his years as an intensive care nurse. His relationship with paper began with patients’ heart rhythms printed from EKG machines. Today, he combines photography, drawing, painting, and paper sculpting to create intricate textures that reflect his understanding of the body, extending his exploration of rhythm and movement into sound and video.

Don’t miss your last chance to visit ‘Vanishing Point’, Hans Op de Beeck’s first solo exhibition with the gallery at Almine Rech Brussels, before it closes on November 7, 2026!
@hans_op_de_beeck
•
One of the essential tensions within Op de Beeck’s work lies between realism and fiction. His sculptures are executed with extraordinary precision and, at first glance, appear strikingly realistic. Yet subtle distortions reveal their constructed nature.
This ambiguity is crucial. It places the viewer in a state of uncertainty where perception can no longer be taken for granted. In this sense, his work possesses an unmistakably theatrical dimension.
His installations function like stage sets: meticulously conceived, lit, and choreographed. Every object plays a role; every space suggests an action unfolding beyond our field of vision. The artist does not create a self-contained reality but a world that constantly points elsewhere—beyond the visible, beyond the immediate.
— Ruud Priem, Head of Department and Curator of Fine Arts at the National Museum of Archaeology, History and Art (MNAHA), Luxembourg. Curator of the exhibition ‘Erwin Olaf & Hans Op de Beeck. Inspired by Steichen’ (2022–2023, National Museum of Archaeology, History and Art, Luxembourg).

item.title: @richardhuntsculptor: Commissioned in 1972 by "Ebony/Jet" publisher John H. Johnson, Richard Hunt's "Expansive C
item.author: @richardhuntsculptor
item.description:
Commissioned in 1972 by "Ebony/Jet" publisher John H. Johnson, Richard Hunt's "Expansive Construction" was a monumental centerpiece installed in the lobby of the Johnson Publishing Company headquarters in Chicago. In a new book, "820 Ebony/Jet: Visions of the Johnson Publishing Company, an American Icon," an essay by the Richard Hunt Legacy Foundation's Executive Director, Jon Ott, explores how Hunt’s welded bronze sculpture served as a powerful visual metaphor for Black aspiration and creative freedom.
This iconic work united three Black visionaries at the peak of their influence: publisher John H. Johnson (who funded Richard Hunt's 1971 MoMA retrospective traveling to the Art Institute of Chicago), John W. Moutoussamy (the first Black architect to design a downtown Chicago skyscraper), and rising sculptor Richard Hunt.
Hunt's "Expansive Construction" remains a testament to how biomorphic forms gave voice to African American self-determination and the freedom of the Black imagination. Explore the full essay in "820 Ebony/Jet," with poignant photography by Barbara Karant.
Richard Hunt's "Expansive Construction" is now in the collection of Theaster Gates's foundation. Gates also has thousands of reference library books and objects from the Johnson Publishing archive, much of which is housed at Gates's Stony Island Arts Bank in Chicago.

item.author: @sothebys
item.description:
97 years ago today, this Norman Rockwell illustration graced the cover of The Saturday Evening Post. It’s a clever commentary on the 1920s Jazz Age, and after over 30 years in private hands, it makes its auction debut at #SothebysNewYork.
Rockwell created 321 cover illustrations for The Post over a 47-year period. This work is the final time that James K. Van Brunt, one of Rockwell’s favorite subjects, modeled for the artist. Here, Rockwell depicts him as a violinist enticed to buy a saxophone, a defining symbol of the Jazz Age. In drawing a classical musician tempted by the new instrument of the day, Rockwell sets up the narrative tension and humor which defined his great Post covers.
‘Man Looking at Saxophone (Jazz It Up with a Sax)’ is a highlight of The Modern Day Auction, presented in partnership with @celine. Register to bid in the 19 November sale at the link in bio.

item.title: @pennmuseum: How should international organizations confront cultural heritage preservation as part of
item.author: @pennmuseum
item.description:
How should international organizations confront cultural heritage preservation as part of their missions during modern military conflict?
Dr. Lynn Meskell gets right to the heart of that question with her forthcoming book, “Ruined: The Heritage of War from UNESCO to NATO,” (Oxford University Press, November 2027) as she shines a light on the seizure and destruction of cultural heritage in places such as Gaza and Ukraine—where the past has become weaponized and targeted.
Dr. Meskell is a curator in the Penn Museum’s Middle East and Asia sections, Penn Integrates Knowledge professor, Richard D. Green Professor in Anthropology in the School of Arts and Sciences, Professor in Historic Preservation at the Weitzman School of Design, and a leading researcher in the politics and ethics of cultural heritage.
“Ruined” traces the history of protecting heritage is a requirement for agencies guarding against illicit trafficking, terror financing, cultural cleansing, and crimes against humanity—yet, at the same time, it can be weaponized to push for more conflict. It demonstrates how heritage assets once thought of as “global goods” have now turned into tools of war.

This is how to look at Ed Ruscha’s 1964 painting ‘Dimple.’ With just six letters, Ruscha explores exactly what a word can do in a painting.
Here, Sotheby’s David Galperin analyzes the power of Ruscha’s clamp. ‘Dimple’ is one of only seven paintings featuring his rare and important C-clamp motif, which squeezes the final 'e' here. It radically disrupts the flatness of the text, giving it both a sculptural physicality and surreal bent. With this act of subversion, Ruscha elevates text into object, language into art, colloquialism into critique.

Kahlil Joseph, 2025, 113 min., USA
As America watches the election returns, Maysles Documentary Center invites audiences to experience a different kind of news.
Kahlil Joseph’s BLKNWS: TERMS & CONDITIONS (2025) is a visionary exploration of Black history, memory, and imagination. Combining archival footage, music, contemporary media, and speculative storytelling, Joseph constructs a radical alternative to conventional news and historical narratives, one in which Black life becomes the center rather than the margins of the story.
Co-presented with The New Museum, who presented Khalil Joseph’s exhibition Shadow Play in 2017 and are currently presenting BLKNWS collaborator Arthur Jafa’s major survey exhibition, I Am Tony, the screening highlights artists challenging conventional ways of seeing and representing Black experience, drawing upon the emotional power of images, the rhythms of Black music, and the possibilities of cinema to imagine new forms of collective memory and consciousness.
On a night dominated by electoral maps, political punditry, and competing visions of America’s future, BLKNWS invites us to consider another question: Who gets to tell our stories, and what becomes possible when we control the images?
Join us following the screening for a post-election gathering and celebration at Maysles Documentary Center!

item.title: @blacktheatreunited: 4 years ago, Broadway made history.
item.author: @blacktheatreunited
item.description:
4 years ago, Broadway made history.
On November 1, 2022, the Brooks Atkinson became the Lena Horne Theatre. The first Broadway house ever named for a Black woman.
The renaming was part of BTU’s New Deal for Broadway, where the three major theatre owners each committed to naming at least one of their theatres for a Black artist.
Her name is on 47th Street now. For good.

item.author: @sothebys
item.description:
Instead of dreaming of Hollywood, Greta Lee fantasized about finding her own bohemia. She wanted to be an artist. “I wanted to be part of something cool," she says, "which to me was just about finding a thing that was greater than me and something that I could really get behind in an authentic way.”
By now, her meteoric rise to fame is old news. In 2023, she starred in Celine Song’s “Past Lives” as Nora, a New York-based Korean-Canadian playwright who, two decades after leaving Seoul, reconnects with her childhood sweetheart. What came next was a different kind of career: a sprawl of genres that reads less like a strategy than an appetite, making up for lost time.
